issues.legal_issue: A deed executed as security for a loan, rather than as a genuine sale, does not transfer title when the surrounding evidence establishes the transaction’s true character.
material_facts: The property owner received a loan and executed a deed in favour of the lender, with an agreement for reconveyance if repayment was made.
The lender’s side admitted that the money was a loan and that the deed was given as security.
The evidence included an agreement for reconveyance, and the stated sale price was substantially below the property’s earlier purchase price.
issues.conclusion: The deed was only security for a loan and did not transfer title to the lender.
issues.legal_principle: The nature of the transaction is determined from the deed and the evidence as a whole, including admissions and any contemporaneous reconveyance agreement. A security transaction is not a genuine sale merely because it is recorded in a sale deed. The Court relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this characterization.

rule.if: ownership_declaration_suit and loan_advanced and deed_given_as_security and reconveyance_agreed and consideration_below_property_value

predicates.ownership_declaration_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking a declaration of ownership based on the asserted true character of a property transaction.
predicates.loan_advanced: One party advanced money to the property owner as a loan.
predicates.deed_given_as_security: The parties used a deed over the property to secure repayment rather than to make a genuine sale.
predicates.reconveyance_agreed: The parties agreed that the property would be conveyed back upon repayment.
predicates.consideration_below_property_value: The stated sale consideration was substantially below the property’s value or a relevant prior purchase price.

issues.definition: When an ownership declaration suit concerns a deed given to secure a loan, and the parties agreed to reconveyance while the stated consideration was substantially below the property’s value, the deed did not transfer title.

issues.legal_issue: A transferee cannot acquire title under a subsequent sale from a seller who had no title to the property.
material_facts: The lender had acquired no title under the deed that was given only as security for a loan.
The lender later executed a registered sale deed in favour of the subsequent purchasers.
The lender’s name had been entered in the revenue records, but that entry did not establish title.
issues.conclusion: The subsequent sale did not confer title on the purchasers because the seller had no title to convey; the revenue entry did not change that result.
issues.legal_principle: A transferor cannot convey a better title than the transferor possesses. Mutation or an entry in revenue records does not itself confer title in the absence of an underlying transfer of title. The Court cited no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this holding.

predicates.subsequent_property_sale: A person later transferred the property to another purchaser.
predicates.seller_lacked_title: The person making the later transfer had not acquired title to the property.
predicates.revenue_entry_without_underlying_title: A revenue record showed the seller’s name, but no underlying transaction had given the seller title.

issues.definition: If a person makes a subsequent property sale without having acquired title, a revenue entry alone does not enable the purchaser to acquire title.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court may reappraise evidence in a second appeal and reverse purported concurrent findings when the lower appellate court failed to properly assess the evidence and the reversal involves a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The dispute reached the High Court in a second appeal, and the High Court formulated a substantial question of law about whether the deed conveyed title.
The trial court dismissed the suit, while the first appellate court affirmed the result without properly discussing the evidence or resolving the trial court’s framed issues.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and reversed the lower courts’ decisions.
No attempt was made at the High Court hearing to have another substantial question of law formulated.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in reappraising the evidence and reversing the lower courts’ decisions; the challenge to its exercise of second-appeal jurisdiction failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs second appeals. Under Section 100(5), the appeal is heard on the formulated substantial question of law, subject to the court’s stated power to hear another such question for reasons recorded. Where the lower appellate court has not properly assessed the evidence, its affirmance does not constitute a sound concurrent factual finding that prevents the High Court from reaching its own conclusion. Mohan Lal v. Nihal Singh was distinguished; Thiagarajan v. Sri Venugopalaswamy B. Koil was distinguished because no further question was sought to be formulated at the hearing.

rule.if: second_appeal and substantial_question_formulated and first_appeal_failed_to_assess_evidence and (mechanical_concurrent_findings or no_reasoned_factual_review)

predicates.second_appeal: The matter came before the High Court as a second appeal.
predicates.substantial_question_formulated: The High Court formulated a substantial question of law for the second appeal.
predicates.first_appeal_failed_to_assess_evidence: The first appellate court failed to properly discuss or assess the evidence and issues before it.
predicates.mechanical_concurrent_findings: The first appellate court mechanically affirmed the trial court’s findings.
predicates.no_reasoned_factual_review: The lower appellate decision did not provide a reasoned review of the factual record.

issues.definition: In a second appeal with a formulated substantial question of law, if the first appeal failed to assess the evidence and the lower courts’ apparent concurrence was mechanical or unreasoned, the High Court may reappraise the evidence and reverse.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court need not disturb a High Court judgment that corrects manifestly unreasonable and unjust findings reached through improper appreciation of the evidence.
material_facts: The case came before the Supreme Court as a civil appeal challenging the High Court’s reversal of the lower courts.
The lower courts had not properly appreciated the oral and documentary evidence, and the High Court had corrected their unreasonable and unjust conclusions.
The Supreme Court found no basis to interfere with the High Court’s judgment.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the High Court’s judgment and decree.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution does not expressly fetter the Supreme Court’s power to interfere with concurrent findings of fact; that power is exercised sparingly, but the Court may correct grave injustice. The number of times a finding has been affirmed is not decisive if it is manifestly unreasonable and unjust in light of the evidence. The Court relied on Smt. Indira Kaur v. Sheo Lal Kapoor.

rule.if: supreme_court_civil_appeal and lower_courts_misappreciated_evidence and findings_manifestly_unreasonable_or_unjust and high_court_corrected_injustice

predicates.supreme_court_civil_appeal: A civil appeal from a High Court judgment was before the Supreme Court.
predicates.lower_courts_misappreciated_evidence: The lower courts failed to properly appreciate the evidence relevant to their findings.
predicates.findings_manifestly_unreasonable_or_unju: The findings reached by the lower courts were manifestly unreasonable or unjust in light of the evidence.
predicates.high_court_corrected_injustice: The High Court reversed the lower courts’ findings to correct the resulting injustice.

issues.definition: When a civil appeal presents lower-court findings that are manifestly unreasonable or unjust because of improper appreciation of evidence, and the High Court has corrected that injustice, the Supreme Court leaves the High Court judgment undisturbed.
